1.title: A Foot in Both Camps

lines.text: Welcome back to Elsewhere, the podcast for people who aren't quite sure where they're from. I'm Leila, and with me, as ever, is Marco, who has just moved back to Melbourne after twelve years in London. Marco, how's it going?
Honestly? It's weird. I'm loving being near my family again, but I'm feeling a bit like a fish out of water. Which is ridiculous, because I grew up here.
It's not ridiculous at all. Reverse culture shock is a real thing. What's been the strangest part?
The small stuff. People keep saying I sound like a Pom now. My nephew, who's nine, was imitating me at dinner. And I've been finding myself apologising for things nobody here apologises for.
That's so English of you.
I know! I was being polite to a parking meter yesterday. Actually said 'sorry' to it.
So where do you feel you belong now? Here, there, both?

I think I've got a foot in both camps, and that's not always comfortable. When I was in London, I was always the Aussie. Now I'm here, I'm the one who's gone a bit English. You stick out like a sore thumb in both places, just in different ways.
I hear that from so many listeners. But I wonder whether it's also a kind of freedom. You're not stuck being one thing.
Maybe. I'm thinking about it differently than I did a month ago, for sure. At first I was seeing it as a loss. Now I'm wondering whether I've just gained an extra home.
Have you met anyone else in the same boat?
Funnily enough, yes. There's a guy at work who spent ten years in Berlin. We had lunch and within five minutes we were finishing each other's sentences. A real kindred spirit.
That's lovely. So are you going to put down roots this time?
That's the plan. I've been looking at flats near the beach. Though my mum is being very unsubtle about wanting me within walking distance of her.
Mums tend to be. Listeners, if you've moved back somewhere you once called home, we'd love to hear how you're finding it. Marco, any last words?
Just that it gets easier. I think. Ask me again in six months.

1.title: Tracing a Family Name
1.focus: Past tenses for distancing and politeness

lines.text: Good morning, County Records Office, Hugh speaking.
Oh, hello. Good morning. I was wondering if you might be able to help me. I'm trying to trace my great-grandfather, who I believe emigrated from your area around nineteen-ten.
Certainly, I'll do my best. Do you have a name?
Yes, Thomas Breen. I was hoping you might have some record of him, a baptism, a school register, anything really.
Breen. That's quite a common name round here, I'm afraid. Do you know which parish he came from?
Not exactly. Family stories said it was a village near the coast. I did think it might be somewhere called Kilmore, but I'm not certain.
That narrows it down a little. There are two Kilmores in the county, as it happens. Did he leave alone, or with family?

Alone, as far as we know. He was eighteen. And this is the slightly awkward part. My grandmother always said he'd been disowned by his father. Nobody knew why. I wanted to ask whether records like yours might shed any light on that sort of thing.
Ah. Well, we wouldn't usually have anything as personal as that, I'm afraid. But sometimes court records or parish notes mention family disputes. It's a long shot, but it's not impossible.
That would be wonderful. I'd really appreciate it if you could look.
Of course. I was going to suggest, actually, that you send us an email with everything you know. Dates, names, any letters. It makes the search much easier.
I'll do that today. Can I ask, roughly how long would it take?
Usually a couple of weeks. And there's a small search fee, which I'll include in my reply.

That's absolutely fine. I just wanted to say, it means a lot. My family's always felt a bit rootless. We've moved so often. I suppose I'm looking for some sense of belonging, even if it's a hundred years late.
You'd be surprised how many people say exactly that. I hope we find him for you, Mrs Breen.
Thank you so much. You've been very kind.

2.title: Anatomy of a Speech

lines.text: Last night's conference speech by the opposition leader has already produced one sound bite that's everywhere this morning: 'We will not be the generation that looked away.' Professor David Lane studies political rhetoric. Professor, why has that line struck such a chord?

Well, what makes it work is the structure. It's a negative, it's about identity, and it's in the future. It doesn't promise any specific policy. What it does is invite the audience to imagine being judged by their grandchildren. That's very powerful.
Some critics say it's just spin. All emotion, no substance.

I'd be careful there. It's true that the line itself contains no policy. But it was the passage immediately afterwards, on housing, that contained the actual proposals. The sound bite is the hook. Whether the proposals stand up is a separate question.
What else did you notice?

The use of three. She did it repeatedly. 'Not for the few, not for the lucky, not for the loud.' It's one of the oldest techniques there is. What the rule of three does is give a sense of completeness. Two items feel like a comparison. Four feel like a list. Three feel like a conclusion.
Did anything fall flat?

There was one moment, yes. She said her party had always defended public services. Now, given the record, a lot of listeners will have heard that as paying lip service rather than as a serious claim. It's when a speaker overreaches like that that audiences stop trusting the rest.
And her delivery?
Very controlled. What I found interesting was how often she paused. Not after the big lines, before them. It creates anticipation. You lean in.
Is there a risk that we, the media, focus too much on technique and not enough on content?

Absolutely, and I'm part of the problem. It's the policies, not the rhetoric, that will actually affect people's lives. But rhetoric is how policies reach people. Ignore it, and you don't understand why some ideas spread and others don't.
Professor Lane, thank you.

questions.explain_es: "What it does is invite the audience to imagine being judged by their grandchildren."

2.title: Did You Twist My Words?
2.focus: Inversion after negative and restrictive adverbials

lines.text: Joining me are Joanna Reid, the journalist whose report on the Greenfield housing company has caused such a stir, and Kevin Doyle, the company's head of communications. Kevin, you've alleged that the report was deliberately misleading.

I have, and I won't mince my words. Never in twenty years of working with the press have I seen a story so selectively edited. Ms Reid took a forty-minute interview with our chief executive and used eleven seconds of it.
Eleven seconds in which he said, and I quote, 'Safety inspections are a box-ticking exercise.' I didn't twist his words. I reported them.
Out of context. What he went on to say was that inspections should be more rigorous, not less. That's the opposite of what your piece insinuated.
I'd refute that. The full transcript is on our website. Anyone can read it. Not once did I suggest he opposed inspections. I reported that he'd described them dismissively, which he did.
Kevin, will you concede that the quote is accurate?
I'll concede that he said those words, yes. But only when you hear the whole answer do you understand what he meant. Leaving that out is, frankly, disingenuous.
With respect, we published the full answer online the same day. Little did I expect the company to complain about a transcript it had approved.
You approved it?
The transcript, yes. Not the edit.
Joanna, do you accept any criticism?
I'd accept that the headline was sharper than I'd have written. Headlines aren't written by reporters. But rarely have I been so confident in a story's accuracy.
And Kevin, what would satisfy the company?
A correction making clear what he actually proposed. Nothing more.
If there's a factual error, we'll correct it. So far, nobody has identified one.
We'll leave it there. Thank you both.

3.title: What Did We Actually See?
3.focus: Modals of speculation and deduction (present, past, future)

lines.text: Oscar, the police officer's just rung. She wants us both to give statements about the accident this afternoon. Can you remember what colour the van was?
White. Definitely white. Well, I think so. I only caught a glimpse of it before it turned the corner.
I thought it was grey. Silver, maybe.
Hmm. It can't have been silver. I'd have noticed. Silver catches the light.
It was overcast, though. It might easily have looked white to you and grey to me.
True. Okay. What about the cyclist? Did you see whether he went through the red light?
That's the thing. I'm racking my brains and I genuinely can't discern whether the light was red or amber. I was looking at my phone, then I heard the brakes.
Same, more or less. I was looking at the café menu. I've got a gut feeling the cyclist was in the right, but I couldn't swear to it.
You must have seen something, though. You were facing the junction.
I was facing it, but that's not the same as watching it. I think my brain's filling in the gaps. Every time I replay it, I get a slightly different version.
Maybe we should write down what we remember separately, before we talk any more. Otherwise we'll end up agreeing on a story that might not be true.
Good idea. The officer will probably ask us that anyway. They'll have seen this a thousand times.
Do you think the cyclist will be okay?
He was sitting up and talking when the ambulance came, so he can't have been too badly hurt. He'll be sore tomorrow, I should think.
I hope so. Right, pen and paper. No conferring.
No conferring. Although, for the record, the van was white.
Oscar!

3.title: Why We See What We Expect
3.focus: Needn't have vs didn't need to; should have, might have, could have

lines.text: Let me start with a confession. Last year I bought a house. Before I signed, a surveyor told me the roof would need replacing within five years. I didn't want to hear it. I loved the house. So I found a second surveyor, who said the roof was fine, and I believed him. Guess what I'm paying for this spring.

That, in a nutshell, is confirmation bias: the tendency to seek out and believe information that supports what we already want to think. And here's the uncomfortable part. Knowing about it doesn't protect you. I teach this stuff. I still fell for it.
With the benefit of hindsight, I should have listened to the first surveyor. I could have negotiated a lower price. I might even have walked away. Instead, I let wishful thinking cloud my judgement.

Now, people often ask me how to avoid this. The honest answer is: you can't, entirely. But you can build habits. One is to actively look for evidence against your preferred view. Another is to ask someone who has no stake in the decision.
Can I ask something? You said you got a second opinion. Isn't that what we're supposed to do?

Great question. A second opinion is good if you're genuinely open to it. My problem was that I went looking for a particular answer. I needn't have bothered with the second surveyor at all, really. I'd already decided. I just wanted permission.
So what should you have done?

I didn't need to ignore my feelings. Loving a house is fine. What I should have done was separate the decision from the emotion: write down what would make me walk away, before I fell in love with the place, and stick to it.

We all have blind spots. Mine, clearly, is old houses with big windows. Yours might be a political view, a friend, a favourite sports team. The goal isn't to eliminate bias. It's to notice when it's driving.
Is it worse in some people than others?

Some research suggests people who are very confident in their intelligence can be more susceptible, because they're better at building arguments for what they already believe. Which is a slightly alarming thought for a room full of academics.
So, homework. Next time you make a decision you care about, write down one piece of evidence that would change your mind. If you can't think of one, that's your warning sign.

4.title: Taking the Plunge
4.focus: Advanced verb patterns: gerund vs infinitive with change of meaning

lines.text: Amaya Cruz founded her furniture-repair company five years ago. It now employs sixty people. Amaya, it's been described as a meteoric rise. Does it feel like that?
Not from the inside. From the inside it felt like five years of not sleeping. But I'll take 'meteoric'.
You were working as a lawyer before. What made you take the plunge?

I remember sitting in a meeting about a contract dispute and realising I'd stopped caring about any of it. I'd always loved fixing old chairs, it was my weekend thing. And I thought, if I don't try doing this properly now, I never will.
How did you get a foot in the door? Furniture's a crowded market.

I tried to get into big retailers first, and failed completely. Nobody would take my calls. So I tried offering free repairs to a few cafés in exchange for a little sign saying who'd done it. That worked far better than any advertising.
Were there moments you nearly gave up?

Oh, constantly. The second year was the worst. We'd lost a big client, the van broke down, and I seriously considered cutting my losses and going back to law. I even stopped to look at job adverts one evening. Then a customer emailed to say we'd saved her grandmother's rocking chair, and I closed the laptop.
Do you regret leaving law?
I regret not leaving sooner. I don't regret anything else. Well, I regret to say I've forgotten most of my contract law, but that's probably fine.
What's next for the company?
We're going to expand into two more cities. But I'm conscious of not resting on our laurels. The moment you think you've made it, someone younger and hungrier comes along.
And advice for anyone thinking of doing what you did?
Remember to talk to people who've failed, not just people who've succeeded. You learn far more. And try to keep one foot in reality. Passion's great, but it doesn't pay the rent.

4.title: Cracks in the Glass Ceiling

lines.text: New figures published this morning show a modest increase in the proportion of women on the boards of the country's largest companies. But, as our business desk reports, the picture further down the ladder is rather less encouraging.

The headline number is a rise from thirty-one to thirty-four per cent of board seats held by women over the last two years. That's real progress, albeit slow. The more revealing figure, though, is the representation of women in senior executive roles, the people actually running the companies day to day. There, the improvement is barely measurable.
Why the difference?

Board appointments are highly visible and subject to considerable public pressure. Executive promotion happens through internal processes that are far less transparent. Companies have made headway on the first while the second has largely stalled.
We spoke to a director at one of the firms named in the report.

The introduction of targets for boards was a make-or-break moment. Without them, I doubt we'd have seen any change. But the glass ceiling hasn't disappeared. It's just moved. Women reaching middle management are still falling by the wayside at a far higher rate than men.
What explains that attrition?

A combination of factors. The concentration of senior roles requiring long hours and constant availability. The absence of flexible working at senior level. And, frankly, the persistence of informal networks, the golf, the after-work drinks, from which a lot of women are effectively excluded.
The report recommends the extension of reporting requirements to executive teams, which would at least make the scale of the problem visible. Several industry bodies have already expressed support.
And the government's response?
A statement welcoming the findings, with a commitment to a review. Critics point out that a similar review was announced three years ago.
Thank you both.

5.title: A Breakthrough, Purportedly
5.focus: Advanced passives: reporting passives and passive infinitives

lines.text: A blood test that can purportedly detect more than twenty types of cancer before symptoms appear is said to have produced promising results in a large trial. The test is reported to have identified cancers in around half of the participants who were later diagnosed, many of them at an early stage. Our health correspondent, Dr Meera Patel, is with me. Meera, how significant is this?

Potentially very significant, but I'd stress 'potentially'. Early detection is known to improve survival for many cancers, so a test like this could, in theory, save a great many lives. But the technology is still in its infancy, and these results have yet to be published in a peer-reviewed journal.
Half sounds rather low.

It is, and that's important. It means the test missed around half of the cancers that were there. The concern is that a negative result might give people false reassurance. They might be less likely to go to the doctor if they notice symptoms later.
And false positives?

Those are thought to be relatively rare in this trial, which is encouraging. But even a small percentage of false alarms, across millions of people, would mean a lot of anxiety and a lot of unnecessary further tests.
We also spoke to Professor James Grant, an epidemiologist who was not involved in the study.

I think the jury is still out. The test appears to have been tested mostly on people at higher risk. Whether it performs as well in the general population remains to be seen. Claims like this need to stand up to scrutiny before anyone starts talking about national screening.
The company behind the test is understood to be seeking approval in several countries. Meera, when might patients see it?
Not for several years, I'd say. Regulators will want to see far more data. It's an exciting development, but it's one step on a long road.
Dr Meera Patel, thank you.

questions.explain_es: Pasiva de reporte + infinitivo perfecto: 'is reported to have identified'.

5.title: Editing Our Children?
5.focus: Causatives: have/get something done; have someone do

lines.text: Our question tonight: should parents ever be allowed to have their embryos genetically edited? Felix, you're a geneticist. Where do you stand?

For serious inherited diseases, I think there's arguably a case. If a couple both carry a gene for a devastating condition, and they could have it corrected before pregnancy, it's hard to say that's wrong. It's not so different from having a child vaccinated.

I'd disagree with that comparison. A vaccine protects one child. An edit to an embryo is passed on to every future generation. Nobody can give informed consent on behalf of people who don't exist yet.
That's a fair point. But we make decisions affecting future generations all the time. Climate policy, for one.

Yes, and look how well that's gone. My worry is the slippery slope. It starts with serious disease. Then people want their children's height adjusted, or their intelligence boosted. Wealthy parents will have it done abroad if it's banned here.
Felix, is that realistic?
Height and intelligence are influenced by thousands of genes. We genuinely don't know how to edit for them, and it would appear we're nowhere near being able to. So the fear is, I'd say, premature.
Premature, but not unreasonable. The technology is moving fast. And the unintended consequences of editing a single gene aren't fully understood. Some genes do more than one thing.
I agree on that. Which is why any use should be tightly regulated. I'd have every case reviewed by an independent panel.
And who sits on the panel? This is an ethical minefield. Scientists shouldn't be the only ones deciding.
Is there anything you agree on?
That we shouldn't let it happen in secret.
Yes. And that we should get the public involved now, before the decisions are made for us.
We'll leave it there.

6.title: Wolves in the Glen?

lines.text: Right, if everyone gathers round. What you're looking at is twenty years of rewilding. When the estate was bought, this whole hillside was bare. Sheep had grazed it for two centuries. If they hadn't been removed, you'd still be looking at grass and bracken today.
It looks pretty pristine now. Was it planted?

Some of it. But most of these birches seeded themselves. The seeds were in the soil all along. They just never got the chance. Had the deer numbers not been brought down, though, even these wouldn't have survived. Deer eat the young shoots.
So who controls the deer? There aren't any predators here, are there?

Not natural ones, no. That's the big debate. Wolves are what's called a keystone species. If we still had them, the deer would behave very differently. They'd avoid open valleys, keep moving, and the trees would recover on their own.
Are you going to bring wolves back?

I'd love to, honestly. But I wouldn't be allowed to, and the local farmers would be furious. Many of them would have lost livestock if wolves had been reintroduced when the project started. So for now, we cull the deer ourselves. It's not ideal, but otherwise the woodland would never have replenished.
Has anything surprised you?

The speed. I thought it would take fifty years to see real change. Within ten, we had red squirrels back, and golden eagles nesting on that crag. If you'd told me that at the start, I wouldn't have believed you.
Does it make any difference on a bigger scale? It's one estate.

On its own, it's a drop in the ocean. But there are dozens of projects like this now, and together they're becoming a serious carbon sink. And people come to see it, which matters. If nobody had ever seen what's possible, nobody would be asking for more.
Fair enough.
Right, let's head up to the viewpoint. Mind the stream, it's deeper than it looks.

6.title: Before the Tipping Point
6.focus: Inverted conditionals and alternatives to if

lines.text: We're talking about tipping points, thresholds beyond which parts of the climate system may change irreversibly. Dr Lund, how close are we?

Closer than is comfortable. Some ice sheets and some forest systems may be approaching thresholds. Were the Amazon to lose much more of its forest, parts of it could shift towards savannah, and that would turn a carbon sink into a carbon source.
Tariq, you work on policy. Is the message getting through?
Partly. The problem is that a tipping point sounds like a cliff edge, a single date. It isn't. It's more like a zone of risk. Should governments wait for certainty, they'll be too late.
Exactly. But for the scientific uncertainty, I suspect action would have been faster. Politicians use 'we're not sure' as a reason to delay, when it should be a reason for caution.
What can actually be done to stave off the worst?

Cut emissions, obviously. But also protect what's already working. Peatlands, mangroves, old forests. Supposing we stopped deforestation tomorrow, that alone would make a huge difference. It's cheaper to keep a forest than to replant one.
And deal with problems early. With forest fires, for instance, if you nip them in the bud with good monitoring, you avoid disasters that are almost impossible to control later.
Some listeners will say their own actions are a drop in the ocean.
Individually, they are. Provided enough people act together, they aren't. And individual choices shape what politicians think is possible.
I'd add that despair is a luxury. Were we to give up now, we'd guarantee the outcome we fear.
On that note, thank you both.
